title: Bengaluru's Humyn Labs Raises $47 Million to Feed US Robotics Firms Training Data
excerpt: The Series A combines $26 million in Accel-led equity with $21 million in venture debt, backing a Bengaluru startup that records everyday human tasks in more than 20 countries to train robots.
body:
• Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing: $26 million in equity led by Accel and $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton Growth Debt Fund II, TechCrunch reported.
  • The startup records people performing everyday tasks on its own two-camera hardware across more than 20 countries in Latin America and Asia — with Brazil, India and South Korea as its main hubs — and sells the labelled footage as training data for robots and AI models.
  • Humyn says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs and robotics companies, and that about 90% of its revenue comes from the United States; it generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has a further $20 million in signed contracts.
  • For India's tech workforce, the round is another marker of the country becoming a collection hub for "physical AI" data — work that also raises privacy and consent questions when recording happens inside people's homes.

Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to supply U.S. AI and robotics companies with the real-world data they need to train models that operate in physical environments, TechCrunch reported on Wednesday.

The financing comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance's Finserv Intelligence and the Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading and angel investor Anita Pramoda. The remaining $21 million is venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton Growth Debt Fund II, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

What Humyn sells

Robots that can perform everyday human tasks need large volumes of quality data about how people actually move and handle objects, and collecting it remains difficult. Humyn has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks, then uses software to process and label the footage — tracking hand movements, interactions with objects and other details so AI models can learn from it, co-founder Manish Agarwal told TechCrunch.

The company records people doing their usual work or household chores rather than staged activities, working with local partners who identify collection sites and oversee the process. It captures activity across factories, warehouses, farms and homes, converting sight, sound, motion and touch into training-ready data, according to reporting by Business Standard. Startups including Mecka AI, XDOF and MicroAGI are tackling the same data problem, TechCrunch noted.

"Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem."

— Manish Agarwal, co-founder, Humyn Labs, to TechCrunch

The numbers so far

Agarwal, the former chief executive of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February 2026 with Ishank Gupta, a former executive at brewing company AB InBev. The two previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN, whose contributor network across emerging markets helps Humyn collect data, the founders told TechCrunch.

The startup says it has 12 paying customers — frontier AI labs, robotics companies and developers of world models — and that about 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, declining to name the customers. It generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal said, with a further $20 million in deals not yet finalized. Business Standard reported an annualised revenue run rate of more than $50 million within six months of starting operations. Humyn has 51 full-time employees, most of them based in Bengaluru, plus local partners in the countries where it collects data.

Why a third of the round is debt

The $21 million venture debt component reflects how the business pays for its data. Humyn pays workers and data-collection partners daily or weekly, but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payment from its AI lab customers, Agarwal told TechCrunch. Borrowing bridges that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.

What the money is for

The fresh capital will support deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, expand the company's data-capture hardware and enrichment capabilities, and strengthen its presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul, Agarwal told Business Standard. The company plans dedicated robot deployment centres — "robot gyms," in Agarwal's phrase — where models and hardware can be tested in real-world settings, because, he said, providing data alone is not enough for deployment readiness. He added that India is not an immediate priority for commercial robot deployment, because the cost economics of robots do not yet work across several use cases there.

The questions around the model

India has emerged in recent months as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, tapping the country's large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. The practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes, TechCrunch reported. Agarwal said Humyn collects data from people doing their usual work or chores instead of staged activities, supervised by local partners: "The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input," he told TechCrunch.
